style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: The rebuttal paragraph.
So far, we learned the argument paragraph. How we argue for our side, and explain it.
Now, we deal with the other side's view.
So what's the rebuttal paragraph for? To discuss the issue from the other position's point of view. And to show how we deal with one of its arguments.
For the rater, it's pretty much the same. We show that we know the other view, and how we deal with it.
But above all, what we really want to show here is critical thinking.
And that's exactly what the official guide lists under critical thinking: examining the issue from several perspectives, and contending with opposing viewpoints.
In an argument paragraph, we're standing on a stage, giving a speech. Here's our argument, here's why it supports our position. Great.
But nobody hits back. Nobody on the other side says: wait, your argument has a problem. It creates another problem.
So the critical thinking you can show there is high, but only up to a point. You're debating alone.
In the rebuttal paragraph, we're in a real debate. There's an argument from the other side saying: look, the other side has advantages. Or: your side has problems.
And we have to be able to deal with that.
Students ask: do I have to write a rebuttal paragraph? Can the essay have only argument paragraphs for my side?
Well, you don't have to do anything. You can write an essay with only arguments for your side, and not mention the other view at all.
But then you've missed part of what's checked. Being able to see other points of view, and to deal with the other position and its arguments.
So you shouldn't expect a full score if you skip dealing with the other side.
And one more thing. Mentioning the other side isn't the same as answering it.
A sentence like 'Some people disagree, but I still think my view is better' does very little. It names their side, and answers nothing.
What you need is the other side's reason. And an explanation of why that reason does, or doesn't, justify their conclusion.
Now, what the paragraph is made of. We start with a counter-argument.
And it's important to say this right away. We deal with a counter-argument, not with the opposing position.
So we don't write: 'On the other hand, some people oppose installing the cameras.' That's their position. We're not presenting their position.
We present their argument, or one of their arguments. They're against the cameras because of the harm to privacy. Or because of the risk that the database will leak.
It's a key sentence, just like in our argument paragraph. Who gains and what they gain, or who loses and what they lose.
So who loses here? People. And what do they lose? They might be harmed by a leak from the database of images.
Which counter-argument do we choose? A main one. A substantial one.
One option is to take an argument from the task itself. If it's in the task, it's substantial and respectable enough for the rebuttal paragraph.
If not, we choose another main argument.
Choose the strongest argument that you know how to weaken well.
I'd rather choose one that's a bit weaker, but still main, still substantial, that I can weaken with a good, strong weakening that shows high critical thinking.
Rather than take the strongest argument I can find, when all I have against it is 'but my arguments are more important', with no real way to explain it. That's a weakening that doesn't work.
We choose a main argument, and we also develop it. We explain it.
And more than that. Explain it as close to perfectly as you would if it were an argument for your side.
Why? Two reasons. One: it tells the rater I'm not running away. I didn't pick a weak argument that's easy to weaken.

I understand my position has disadvantages. I understand the other side has serious arguments. I took all that into account, and when I weigh everything I know, my advantages outweigh the disadvantages. That came from thinking, not from 'this is what I feel like'.
Two: look through the rater's eyes. He sees a strong counter-argument, explained really well, and he's almost convinced. And then I manage to weaken it. Wow.
It's easy to reject a claim after you make it sound selfish or foolish. That shows very little. You can disagree firmly, without pretending the other side has no reasonable concern.
And, a little paradoxically, explaining their argument well actually helps you weaken it.
Once we explain why they claim it, we create more places to find a weak point. More links in the explanation, where one of them might be weak.
When I have a logical chain, it's much easier to pick a weak point and attack it. And that way, I weaken the whole argument.
A bare, short argument with no explanation is harder to weaken.
So write their chain, develop it fairly in the paragraph, and now every arrow is a possible target.
After we chose a counter-argument and explained it, we get to the weakening.
In the first part of the weakening, we express some reservation about the counter-argument.
We don't say: okay, this counter-argument is right. Full stop. Then there's no weakening. No confrontation. We didn't really deal with the other side.
Now notice. Sometimes we accept the counter-argument, and say it's true. So how can we still have a reservation?

That's fine. Even if the argument is true, I can have a reservation about the argument, or the position. It's true, but it causes another problem, or it has some other flaw. It's true in theory, but some people will bypass it, or won't do what's expected.
We covered all these options in the types of weakenings.
Then we weaken it. And the weakening is done with an argument. Just like there's an argument paragraph and a counter-argument, there's an argument that weakens the counter-argument.
And of course, that argument has to be explained. Why does my argument weaken theirs?
And your reply has to hit their actual problem. Ask yourself: what is the other side worried will happen? And how does my reply deal with that?
If they're afraid of a leak from the database, and you answer 'but cameras reduce crime', you haven't touched their worry. You just repeated your side.
And if you offer a safeguard or an alternative, it only helps if you explain how it works.
Notice that in both the counter-argument and the weakening, I wrote support as optional.
Remember from the argument paragraph. A key sentence, the argument in short. Development, its explanation. And support, making the explanation stronger with an example or a comparison.
So why is it optional here? Because this is an essay in an exam. There are limits, on time and on length.
If we add support everywhere, we might not finish the essay. Or we might run past the lines on the answer sheet.
It depends on the essay. If you see there's room to add support, add it. That's excellent.
The paragraph opens with a fitting connector. One that shows contrast.
Until now we talked about our arguments. Argument paragraph one, argument paragraph two. Now I'm telling the reader: I'm switching to the other side.
And in the weakening, too, we need fitting connectors. Including a word of concession.
Something like: 'Admittedly, there may be some harm to privacy; however, the right to life and security...'
A few more notes.
First, we weaken, we don't refute. It sounds like just a word, but it changes how you think.
Refuting means saying something isn't true. Here there's no right and wrong. There are two sides, two positions. Each one is legitimate, and each has advantages and disadvantages.
So our aim is to weaken the counter-argument. Not to prove it's false.
Even when you show that an argument does not hold, you show it with a fact, and you hedge it. 'Largely does not hold in this case', not 'is simply false'.
And one way to do that is to write in a qualified way. It is likely that. This may cause. This could lead to.
Next, avoid empathetic wording. Not 'I understand them', but 'there is some logic in their argument'.
We talk to the mind, not to the feelings. This is academic writing.
Some students use fixed phrases all through the essay. And in the rebuttal paragraph especially.
Like: 'Admittedly, there is some truth in this; however...' That's fine.
But not all weakenings are the same. So you can't always use the same phrase.
'Admittedly, there is some truth in this' says: the argument is true, or partly true.

But sometimes I want to say the argument doesn't hold. Then I'll write: 'At first glance, this argument seems logical; however, it does not take into account...' and then some point that only I noticed.
So, prepare fixed phrases, that's recommended. But have different ones for different types of weakening.
And at the end, like in every paragraph, rewrite and raise the level of the language. To pick up a few more points on the language rubric.
